video_title: MacroVoices #554 Dr. Anas Alhajji + Louis-Vincent Gave: Developing Crises in Middle-East and France
gist: Double-header: Anas Alhajji, just back from Riyadh Energy Week, argues the 'three seas' crisis (Gulf, Red Sea, Black Sea) is mainly a refined-products and diesel crisis made worse by refinery attacks and Chinese export quotas, and that AI capex and EU subsidies are masking a looming recession. Louis-Vincent Gave says France is in an emerging-market-style debt crisis that threatens the euro through insurers and banks, and recommends a positive-carry short of the euro against peripheral currencies. (The transcript calls this episode 555; the title says 554.)

themes.theme: Three Seas Crisis and Hormuz Bypass Infrastructure

insights.claim: Alhajji frames the current disruption as a 'three seas crisis' spanning the Persian Gulf, Red Sea and Black Sea, which he says has permanently changed energy markets and also hit fertilizer and agricultural trade.
insights.speaker: Dr. Anas Alhajji
insights.so_what: Treat the disruption as multi-commodity and structural rather than a single-chokepoint event that reverts on a ceasefire.
insights.quote: The three seas crisis, when we talk about the three seas crisis, we are talking about the Gulf, we're talking about the Red Sea, and we are also talking about the Black Sea. And this has changed energy markets and probably forever.

insights.claim: Saudi Arabia expanded the East-West pipeline from 5.5 to 7 million b/d and aims to lift total Hormuz-bypassing export capacity to 10 million b/d, chiefly via a new pipeline through the Empty Quarter to Oman that it believes can be finished in 2-3 years.
insights.speaker: Dr. Anas Alhajji
insights.so_what: Multi-year capex and pipeline/EPC opportunity; over time it structurally cuts the Hormuz risk premium on Saudi barrels.

insights.claim: The planned Oman pipeline is designed as a hub that Iraq and Kuwait could tie into with north-south lines, so Gulf exports would bypass both Hormuz and the Red Sea and go straight to the Arabian Sea and Asia.
insights.speaker: Dr. Anas Alhajji
insights.so_what: A regional bypass grid would reshape Gulf-to-Asia tanker routes and reduce reliance on Red Sea transit.

insights.claim: Saudi Arabia can convert its east-west gas pipeline to carry about 1.2 million b/d of oil in roughly 3-5 weeks during months when it does not need the gas (until May), then switch it back - seasonal optionality on export capacity.
insights.speaker: Dr. Anas Alhajji
insights.so_what: Hidden swing capacity of roughly 1.2 mb/d of bypass exports that most supply models probably miss.

insights.claim: The UAE has already started building a second bypass pipeline despite the war; Alhajji argues attackers are unlikely to waste expensive missiles on early-stage construction rather than the finished asset, so building should not be delayed.
insights.speaker: Dr. Anas Alhajji
insights.so_what: Bypass projects are likely to proceed during the conflict, though finished assets remain targets.

insights.claim: US Energy Secretary Chris Wright said Hormuz crude flows are at 80-90% of pre-conflict levels (about 13-14 million b/d), but refined products are only at 25-35% of pre-crisis levels. Alhajji says the crude figures are noisy and possibly double-counted, but the products gap is real and drives the diesel crisis.
insights.speaker: Dr. Anas Alhajji
insights.so_what: The bottleneck is products, not crude, so the dislocation shows up in cracks and diesel more than in flat-price crude.
insights.quote: only 25 to 35% of products of pre-crisis levels were moving at. And this is where the problem is.

insights.claim: Townsend argues that attacks on refineries in Russia, Saudi Arabia and the UAE are destroying capacity that takes about 10 years to rebuild, which could cause a lasting crack-spread blowout that outlives the wars. Alhajji agrees and says he has written about it for months.
insights.speaker: Erik Townsend / Dr. Anas Alhajji
insights.so_what: Structural long refining margins and diesel cracks; refiners outside the conflict zones are the beneficiaries.
insights.quote: It means the whole world is going to have a crack spread explosion problem that I don't think can be solved until you build new refineries.

insights.claim: Alhajji lists the drivers of the diesel crisis: lost output from Gulf refineries (including Ruwais in the UAE), panic export bans on petroleum products, rerouted ships leaving more product on water, hoarding by traders, and about 800,000 b/d of diesel lost in the Black Sea.
insights.speaker: Dr. Anas Alhajji
insights.so_what: Several overlapping causes mean diesel tightness will not fix itself when any single one is resolved.

insights.claim: Alhajji says the media fixated on the Houthi attack on Saudi Arabia's Jazan refinery, which does not affect crude flows, while largely ignoring the loss of 3 million b/d of crude and of Black Sea diesel until President Trump raised it about a month ago.
insights.speaker: Dr. Anas Alhajji
insights.so_what: Black Sea product losses are under-covered and may be under-priced next to Gulf headlines.

insights.claim: Because the crisis is multi-dimensional and multi-commodity, ending one war (e.g., Iran) will not end the others, and the diesel crisis will persist even after a partial resolution.
insights.speaker: Dr. Anas Alhajji
insights.so_what: Do not price a quick normalization of diesel or cracks on peace headlines.

insights.claim: Paul Sankey (cited by Townsend) says the world's remaining spare refining capacity is mostly in China, and China has signaled a China-first policy on exports of refined products.
insights.speaker: Erik Townsend
insights.so_what: China's export quotas become the marginal swing factor for global product prices.

insights.claim: Alhajji explains that China sets domestic product prices below world prices, so Chinese refiners lose money at home and profit only from exports, which Beijing controls with quotas, including a full export halt in October. He says Europe and California handed China this leverage by closing refineries.
insights.speaker: Dr. Anas Alhajji
insights.so_what: Chinese quota announcements are a key catalyst for crack spreads; Western refinery closures turned China into the swing supplier.
insights.quote: The European leaders basically enabled them. California enabled them by closing those refineries.

insights.claim: Germany's economy minister said at the IEF and World Petroleum Congress that Germany plans to reopen refineries it closed, a reversal of climate-driven policy forced by energy security concerns.
insights.speaker: Dr. Anas Alhajji
insights.so_what: European policy is turning back toward hydrocarbons, which supports refining assets and could mean refinery restarts in Europe.

insights.claim: Townsend's scenario, which Alhajji endorses: crude may never go far above $100 because refinery losses cap how much crude the world can use, while crack spreads go to $200 and diesel reaches $25-30, pushing the economy toward depression. On this view, the trade is the cracks, not flat-price crude.
insights.speaker: Erik Townsend / Dr. Anas Alhajji
insights.so_what: Prefer long cracks / refined-product exposure over outright long crude to express the crisis.
insights.quote: It's the crack spreads that go to the moon.

insights.claim: Townsend notes that backwardation is unwinding as back-month futures rise toward elevated front-month prices, an unusual way for backwardation to resolve, which he reads as the market pricing a long-lasting crisis.
insights.speaker: Erik Townsend
insights.so_what: A rising back of the curve signals a durable supply shock; it supports long-dated producer hedging and long-dated oil exposure.

insights.claim: A poor Indian monsoon has produced what Alhajji recalls as India's worst sugarcane crop in about 11 years. With El Niño driving a global sugar crisis, he expects cane to be diverted from ethanol to sugar in India and Brazil, causing ethanol shortages and higher fuel prices where ethanol blending is mandated.
insights.speaker: Dr. Anas Alhajji
insights.so_what: Long sugar/ethanol exposure; a further source of gasoline-blend tightness on top of the refining shortfall.

insights.claim: Low river levels in Indonesia are stopping barges from delivering palm oil used for biodiesel, while low European river levels have disrupted barge-borne petroleum products and forced nuclear plant closures that raised diesel use in France.
insights.speaker: Dr. Anas Alhajji
insights.so_what: Weather-driven logistics shocks are making the diesel shortage worse beyond the refining problem.

insights.claim: Turkey's energy minister said electricity demand growth comes not only from AI and data centers but also from a rising number of desalination plants, even in a supposedly water-rich country.
insights.speaker: Dr. Anas Alhajji
insights.so_what: Desalination is an underappreciated source of power demand in the energy-water nexus.

insights.claim: Saudi, OPEC and Aramco leaders at Riyadh Energy Week said there is no energy transition, only 'energy addition', and that 'net zero means zero energy security'. Oil and gas stay at the core while solar and wind are added on top.
insights.speaker: Dr. Anas Alhajji
insights.so_what: Producers are signaling sustained investment in hydrocarbons and pushing back on peak-demand narratives.

insights.claim: Alhajji argues the crisis is speeding up an inward turn in which countries build infrastructure redundancy and diversify suppliers. Both add cost, and switching between domestic and imported energy based on relative prices will create a new kind of volatility that no energy outlook yet includes.
insights.speaker: Dr. Anas Alhajji
insights.so_what: Expect structurally higher energy volatility and costs; consensus outlooks understate both.
insights.quote: None of that is incorporated in any energy markets outlook yet.

themes.theme: Oil Demand, Recession Masking and Macro Cushions

insights.claim: Before the war, the IEA expected US oil demand to grow by 160,000 b/d in 2026 and OPEC by 110,000 b/d. Actual year-over-year US demand growth over the first seven months has been about zero, which Alhajji reads as clear demand decline.
insights.speaker: Dr. Anas Alhajji
insights.so_what: Demand has responded to high product prices more than consensus admits, which caps the crude upside.

insights.claim: Alhajji distinguishes demand destruction, which is permanent, from demand decline, which recovers over time, and says the world is seeing a major decline in oil demand driven by high prices for diesel, gasoline and jet fuel rather than crude.
insights.speaker: Dr. Anas Alhajji
insights.so_what: Whether the drop is decline or destruction decides how fast demand comes back after the crisis.

insights.claim: Alhajji says a recession has so far been masked by hundreds of billions of dollars of AI/data-center investment and by EU fuel subsidies (the transcript says $16 for Q2, apparently missing a unit). He expects a recession once either AI spending stops or subsidies decline.
insights.speaker: Dr. Anas Alhajji
insights.so_what: A slowdown in AI capex is the trigger for the macro downturn; watch hyperscaler capex guidance.
insights.quote: the recession is going to happen no matter what the moment that AI spending is going to stop and those subsidies basically decline.

insights.claim: Airline passenger segments have declined worldwide, and air cargo is the only profitable segment, held up by AI equipment shipments.
insights.speaker: Dr. Anas Alhajji
insights.so_what: Favor air cargo over passenger airlines; cargo strength depends on the AI capex cycle.

insights.claim: Gave says Western governments have spent nine months shielding consumers from the energy shock (telling them to keep consuming), while China tightened sharply and India partly did too. He believes Western governments are now reaching the limit of their ability to keep doing so.
insights.speaker: Louis-Vincent Gave
insights.so_what: Once fiscal cushioning ends, the energy shock reaches Western consumers and earnings with a lag.
insights.quote: I think we are reaching the limit.

insights.claim: Gave points to China returning to buy oil after months of absence and to crack spreads rising daily as signs of stress. He warns that if the crisis lasts into 2027, the question is who gets cut off, and the answer may be the EU rather than frontier economies like Sri Lanka or Pakistan.
insights.speaker: Louis-Vincent Gave
insights.so_what: The market assumes the pain stays in frontier markets; the risk that the EU breaks apart is mispriced.

themes.theme: Geopolitics: China BRI, Arctic Routes and Ukraine Talks

insights.claim: Alhajji argues China benefits from Hormuz staying closed or semi-closed and from Bab el-Mandeb disruption because this advances its Belt and Road Initiative, so China is effectively influencing how and when the war ends.
insights.speaker: Dr. Anas Alhajji
insights.so_what: Do not assume China is pushing for a quick reopening of Hormuz; expect the disruption to last longer.

insights.claim: China and Russia are advancing Arctic maritime cooperation, linking the Maritime Silk Road with Russia's trans-Arctic corridor. China-Russia oil trade via the Northern Sea Route is near record highs in the last two months, as an alternative to Hormuz, Malacca, Bab el-Mandeb and Panama.
insights.speaker: Dr. Anas Alhajji
insights.so_what: Arctic shipping and port infrastructure is a growing strategic theme; it also explains US interest in Greenland.

insights.claim: Alhajji says Trump's push to control Greenland is about Arctic transport routes rather than Greenland's oil, gas or minerals.
insights.speaker: Dr. Anas Alhajji
insights.so_what: Arctic geopolitics is the real driver; Greenland resource plays may be the wrong way to express it.

insights.claim: Alhajji is skeptical of Putin's proposed Trump-Putin-Xi summit that excludes Zelensky, saying nothing moves forward without the EU because the EU backs Zelensky's defiance of Trump.
insights.speaker: Dr. Anas Alhajji
insights.so_what: A low chance of a quick Ukraine settlement means the Black Sea and Russian refinery disruptions continue.

insights.claim: Alhajji observes a pattern: each time Trump pressures Zelensky (including after Trump blamed him for high diesel prices), EU members such as France and the UK board tankers carrying Russian oil, and Zelensky publicly announced a refinery strike within 12 hours of Trump's statement.
insights.speaker: Dr. Anas Alhajji
insights.so_what: European escalation against Russian oil flows tends to follow US de-escalation pressure, which keeps supply risk high.

themes.theme: France Sovereign Debt Crisis and Euro Risk

insights.claim: Gave says France is in what looks like a typical emerging-market debt crisis: deficits of about 5% of GDP, debt in a currency it cannot print, a parliament split into three hostile blocs that cannot pass a budget, and a president in office but not in power with approval in the low teens.
insights.speaker: Louis-Vincent Gave
insights.so_what: French spreads can behave like EM credit; political paralysis prevents fiscal repair.
insights.quote: France has issued a bunch of debt in a currency that we can't print.

insights.claim: France cannot raise more revenue through taxes: receipts are about 44% of GDP versus about 24-25% in the US, which puts France on the wrong side of the Laffer curve, so tax hikes would collect less.
insights.speaker: Louis-Vincent Gave
insights.so_what: Fiscal repair must come from spending cuts, which are politically impossible, so the deficit likely persists.

insights.claim: A majority of French debt is held by foreigners, and owning French bonds has become a career risk for investors because the crisis was so widely predicted, which weakens the buyer base.
insights.speaker: Louis-Vincent Gave
insights.so_what: Foreign buyers are likely to keep leaving, which keeps pushing up the OAT risk premium.

insights.claim: Gave calls it one of the oddest things in the market that rates still price three ECB rate hikes while France is in crisis. He says this will never happen.
insights.speaker: Louis-Vincent Gave
insights.so_what: Positioning for fewer ECB hikes than priced (receiving front-end euro rates) has favorable asymmetry.
insights.quote: the market is still pricing in three rate hikes from ECB. You know, that's that's never going to happen.

insights.claim: Gave says France's only economic ways out are raising the retirement age to 70 or devaluing about 50%, which the euro prevents. No candidate in the presidential election six months away proposes either, while Mélenchon proposes default.
insights.speaker: Louis-Vincent Gave
insights.so_what: No credible fiscal fix is on the political menu, so the tail risk of default or euro exit grows.

insights.claim: Using Christophe Guilluy's three-zone framework, Gave argues that urban elites (zone A) can no longer afford transfers to the suburbs (zone B), which are turning violent, so frightened elites are moving toward the rural party (zone C). He says this is why Marine Le Pen is polling in the mid-40s.
insights.speaker: Louis-Vincent Gave
insights.so_what: A Le Pen win becomes the base case, but she would take power with an empty treasury, so fiscal stress continues.

insights.claim: Italy can sensibly avoid default because about 80% of its debt is held domestically, whereas France's foreign-held debt makes default politically easier, though default alone would not be enough without devaluation or retirement reform.
insights.speaker: Louis-Vincent Gave
insights.so_what: France's foreign ownership raises its default risk relative to Italy, which matters for relative-value BTP vs OAT positions.

insights.claim: A French euro exit or default would hit European insurers and pension funds that hold French debt, along with Japanese and US insurers, and would also strain BNP, Société Générale and Crédit Agricole, which are systemically important and big in derivatives. Gave notes that France has issued more debt than the entire African continent.
insights.speaker: Louis-Vincent Gave
insights.so_what: Contagion runs through insurers and French G-SIBs; these are the equities to hedge or short in a tail scenario.

insights.claim: Unlike 2012, Germany can no longer act as Europe's paymaster: it is losing ground to China industrially, and the AfD openly wants to leave the euro and fix ties with Russia. Inflation also limits how freely the ECB can print money compared with the zero-rate era.
insights.speaker: Louis-Vincent Gave
insights.so_what: A 'whatever it takes' style rescue is less likely than in 2012, so euro breakup tail risk is higher.

insights.claim: Gave says he cannot remember another time with so many large tail risks at once: France, energy, a possible end to the AI capex boom, and a US equity market that is 50% tech and communication services, a record concentration.
insights.speaker: Louis-Vincent Gave
insights.so_what: Hedge convex tails; several binary outcomes make the market fragile.
insights.quote: you now have a US equity market which is 50% tech and communication services, a level of concentration never seen before.

insights.claim: Gave advises against shorting French debt against German debt because it costs about 150bp of negative carry and could be crushed if the ECB monetizes French debt. His preferred hedge is to short the euro against peripheral currencies (NOK, ISK, HUF, GBP), which earns about 150-500bp of positive carry, with ISK at the top of that range.
insights.speaker: Louis-Vincent Gave
insights.so_what: A specific positive-carry hedge for euro-breakup risk.
insights.quote: the smartest trade at this stage is to sell the euro against all the European peripheral currencies.

insights.claim: Gave likes long NOK / short EUR in particular because NOK also hedges an oil price spike. More adventurous ideas: buy EUR/JPY or EUR/CNY volatility, with EUR/CNY vol near record lows, or go long Asian currencies against the euro, on the view that Asian allocators would bring money home in a European crisis.
insights.speaker: Louis-Vincent Gave
insights.so_what: Cheap EUR/CNY vol offers convex exposure to a European crisis.

insights.claim: Ceresna notes the EUFN European financials ETF is up about 57% from the Liberation Day lows versus about 27% for XLF. He proposes an equal-dollar pair, long JPMorgan (~$334.58) and short Deutsche Bank (~$32.39), about 10.3 DB shares per JPM share, with an optional April 16, 2027 DB $36 call (~$2) to cap losses on the short leg.
insights.speaker: Patrick Ceresna
insights.so_what: A specific relative-value trade if French stress hits European banks' outperformance.

insights.claim: Ceresna says the S&P 500 is near 7,700 on its 50-day moving average, about 1% above estimated CTA sell triggers near 7,600. Breadth fell to about 20% while the Mag 7 (35% weight) held the index up, SMH is 16% off its peak, memory stocks are at 6-month lows, and Nasdaq large-spec positioning hit the 100th percentile two weeks ago.
insights.speaker: Patrick Ceresna
insights.so_what: A break below 7,600 could set off systematic selling and the first correction since Q1.

insights.claim: Ceresna sees credit stress moving down the quality ladder: junk spreads are breaking out wider (with CoreWeave cited as a contributor) and the BIZD BDC/private credit ETF has made new lows, even as Treasuries bounce (30-year yields down about 35bp).
insights.speaker: Patrick Ceresna
insights.so_what: Private credit and HY are the weak links; watch for an accident in risky credit.

insights.claim: Ceresna says WTI is near $100 and Brent near $112, while the April 2027 contract rallies steadily as backwardation flattens, yet positioning is only at the 23rd percentile on a 3-year lookback, an 'unloved rally'.
insights.speaker: Patrick Ceresna
insights.so_what: Light positioning leaves room for a positioning-driven breakout that could hit inflation expectations and bonds.

insights.claim: Ceresna says gold is near $4,000 and silver at 2026 lows in a distribution phase; a break of $4,000 targets $3,600-3,800, which he sees as a tactical buy zone. Uranium equities have fallen to 52-week lows with the AI basket even though U3O8 spot is stable.
insights.speaker: Patrick Ceresna
insights.so_what: Specific levels for gold entries; uranium equities trade on AI-basket liquidity, not on the commodity.

insights.claim: Ceresna says copper positioning hit a 10-year high in net length a month ago without a price breakout, and copper is now approaching key support near 640 (July low). A break could force a crowded-long washout.
insights.speaker: Patrick Ceresna
insights.so_what: The crowded long plus deteriorating price is a setup for downside volatility; 640 is the trigger.

insights.claim: Ceresna says the dollar's strength was driven by heavy shorts in EUR, GBP and CAD (0th percentile positioning). The euro's weak bounce suggests more downside and room for DXY toward 103, while USD/JPY just broke out of a three-week range on yen strength.
insights.speaker: Patrick Ceresna
insights.so_what: Euro weakness confirms Gave's short-euro view; watch whether the yen breakout holds.
